also: you ought to be thankful to me

terms.gloss: grateful, thankful (of a person); welcome, pleasing (of a thing)
terms.grammar: adjective: of the person, with ergā or in and the accusative
evidence: Cic. Fam. 5.11.1: cognōvī enim tē grātissimum omnium
Cic. Fam. 1.5a.1: quam grātissimus ergā tē esse cognōscerer
terms.comment: One word for both sides of a kindness: said of a person, grateful; said of a thing, welcome, pleasing (grātum mihi est, see appreciate). The opposite is ingrātus, ungrateful, unwelcome (Lewis & Short).

terms.grammar: phrase: grātiam (singular) habēre, with the dative of the person and quod or an infinitive for the reason
evidence: Ter. Ph. 54: Amō tē, et nōn neglēxisse habeō grātiam.
Traupman 57: tibi habeō magnam grātiam, I am very grateful to you
terms.comment: Latin keeps three things apart: grātiam habēre, to feel grateful; grātiās agere, to say thank you (see give thanks); grātiam referre, to repay a kindness (Lewis & Short, s.v. grātia).

evidence: Publil. D 4: Dīxeris maledicta cūncta, cum ingrātum hominem dīxeris.

phrases.latin: cognōvī enim tē grātissimum omnium, idque numquam dēstitī praedicāre. nec enim tū mihi habuistī modo grātiam, vērum etiam cumulātissimē rettulistī.
phrases.english: for I have found you the most grateful of men, and have never stopped saying so. You haven’t only felt grateful to me, you have repaid me in full measure.

phrases.latin: Sī tibi quid fēcī aut faciō quod placet, Simō, et grātum id fuisse advorsum tē habeō grātiam.
phrases.english: If I have done or am doing anything that pleases you, Simo, and if it was welcome to you, I’m grateful.

phrases.latin: Dīxeris maledicta cūncta, cum ingrātum hominem dīxeris.
phrases.english: Call a man ungrateful and you have called him every bad name there is.
You ought to be thankful to me.

sources: Lewis & Short: gratus · Lewis & Short: gratia
